title: Scale and chassis model — how level-1 kids share a battlefield with level-12 Frames
summary: Full proposal in design/scale-and-chassis.md: two hard-separated maths scales (Frame 12+, Personnel 1-8) with exactly three legal interfaces between them; SF2E's real vehicle rules used as the second chassis type alongside Frames; kids are crew, never targets; Claimant Strikes can't target below Large; dismounted kids get a stated clock instead of an unmakeable save. Includes three fully-statted level-12 chassis and worked maths.
description:
Prompted by a design conversation between Ingram and Flippa (a player who also GMs and reads system maths well), pasted into the session 2026-08-22. Flippa correctly identified that level-1 PCs on a level-12 battlefield 'will just die' and proposed making the kids level-14 monster statblocks with no attacks but extreme evasion. Ingram counter-proposed vehicles as a second chassis type at the same level as Frames, levelling in lockstep, with a sports car explicitly named as a wanted option.

The proposal in design/scale-and-chassis.md builds out Ingram's version, on the reasoning that Flippa's fix puts survivability *in the person* (permanent, can't be lost, spent, chosen, or repaired) whereas the chassis version puts it *in the machine* — which turns the fix into the campaign's resource economy instead of a stat-block patch. Flippa's maths is sound and is acknowledged as such; the divergence is about where the durability lives, not whether her numbers work.

Key content of the proposal:
- **The problem, proven** against real GM Core tables: a level-12 Claimant (+26, 3d10+14) critically hits a level-1 kid (AC 17, 18 HP) on 95% of rolls for ~60 damage, exceeding double max HP and triggering instant death by the massive-damage rule. The kid needs ~770 attack rolls to kill it back.
- **The one principle**: a personnel-scale number never appears on the same side of a comparison as a Frame-scale number. Already stated in data/campaign/ground-roles.json ('a level-1 kid never rolls against a level-12 Claimant's DC') — the proposal extends it to vehicles and the Frame-scale map.
- **Three legal interfaces**: be crew (the chassis's numbers roll); Ground Role check at your own level's DC granting a Frame-scale effect; or a stated clock where a save would be unmakeable.
- **SF2E's real vehicle rules do most of the work**: vehicles are objects with Hardness (= Flippa's 'resistance to anything but mech damage', already RAW), an explicit rule that unlisted saves fall through to the pilot's Piloting check, enclosed vehicles granting greater cover, and a Broken state that creates a warning death-spiral.
- **Two flagged deviations**: Handling DC decoupled from chassis level (a level-12 vehicle would be DC 30, which a level-1 kid at +7 cannot drive; fiction justification is that the Directorate builds for conscripted teenagers, and it pays off as characterful — a commandeered civilian sports car has a *higher* Handling DC than a military APC). And Frame-scale chassis list a Reflex save despite RAW's 'typically only Fortitude', so the chassis dodges at level-12 numbers rather than falling through to a kid's unmakeable check.
- **Three fully-statted level-12 chassis**, calibrated against real published AoN vehicles (Turboglider/Enercycle L1, Enercopter L5): a fragile fast coupe, an armoured carrier, and a field-repair rig whose healing borrows against the existing shared technician-day pool.
- **Targeting made mechanical, not GM fiat**: Scale Disparity (Frame-scale Strikes can only target Large+) plus Marked (loud actions expose your chassis until end of next turn), converting survival from GM leniency into player risk management.

The headline validation: all three chassis survive ~5 area attacks by opposite means (the coupe evades, the carrier absorbs), which fell out of role-appropriate stat picks rather than being reverse-engineered — the check that no option is a trap. And a level-1 Sensor Operator revealing a level-appropriate weakness of 10 contributes ~120 damage over a 4-round fight against a 270 HP Claimant — roughly 44% of its health bar — without ever rolling against a Frame-scale DC. That is the 'non-pilot students must not be second-line' goal expressed as arithmetic.
sourceContext: Ingram pasted a Discord design conversation with Flippa and asked for a proposal with real units and demonstrated maths. Proposal written to design/scale-and-chassis.md; status stays 'new' because Ingram has not yet accepted it.
openSubQuestions: Is Marked purely opt-in, or can a Claimant's abilities apply it? (The latter gives Claimants counter-play against a party that never exposes itself.)
How much technician-day debt is one Field Repair worth? Deliberately not costed — it's a dial on the existing Frame economy and should be set alongside those numbers.
Should the sports car be commandeered rather than issued? Its Handling DC 18 implies it isn't Directorate kit — possible first target for the correspondence/negotiation system.
Whether the three named chassis keep these placeholder names, and whether chassis need their own schema (no weapon/equipment/vehicle schema exists in data/schema/ yet).

Now that vehicles are a full parallel progression path, what does the acquisition economy look like — are chassis bought with credits, negotiated for in-fiction, salvaged from the field, or all three?
If a player invests almost entirely in vehicles and barely touches their Frame, does anything in the campaign structure break? (Day 1 and Day 6 both assume specific numbers of Frames launching.)
resolvedSubQuestions: Do chassis level automatically with Frames? — YES, automatic lockstep (2026-08-22). Keeps every comparison intra-scale permanently.

Can a kid hold a chassis in reserve while piloting a Frame? — YES, and further: vehicles are a FULL PARALLEL PROGRESSION PATH. Players can find, buy, and upgrade vehicles exactly as they do Frames, and 'some players might hardly bother with frames.' This is a significant scope expansion beyond the original proposal — the vehicle layer is not a support tier, it is a second viable way to play the whole campaign.

Should chassis classes feel dramatically different? — YES, lean hard into it. Worked example given: a helicopter with by far the greatest speed, the lowest Hardness, high Reflex, and critically low Fortitude. Chassis identity should be felt as a distinct combat experience, not a stat delta.
A fourth balancing axis was added: VISION — see the separate vision-as-chassis-axis idea (accepted).

Two-actions-vs-three-actions contradiction (from day-1-the-fight.json's flagged note) — RESOLVED, 2026-08-22, and it needed no new rule: config.json's Resonance band table already gives Dead Weight/Nominal 2 actions and Harmonised/Absolute 3. The Day 1 pilot starts Harmonised (3 actions), which is the stated exception line 201 always described; line 193's 'two actions' was describing the campaign's normal texture, not scene 7 specifically. See design/scale-and-chassis.md §7.

A fifth axis was added: STAKES. Damage-state degradation (both Frames and vehicles get mechanically worse as they take damage — action cap tied to HP band, echoing how Resonance already caps a pilot's actions) plus a genuinely unlimited-supply 'Runabout' chassis tier, always available with no real stakes if lost. See design/scale-and-chassis.md §8 and §8a.

Vehicles were just as capable as the Frame at direct damage in the first simulated battle (Vesper the helicopter dealt 111 damage vs the Frame's 44) — a real design failure, caught by Ingram asking directly 'why worry about Frames at all?' RESOLVED 2026-08-22 with three composed fixes, all in design/scale-and-chassis.md §14: (a) arrival waves — the city is modeled as 4 miles across, and Speed now decides who's even PRESENT for the first several rounds, not just who hits first; (b) Scale-Hardness 15 on Claimants, applied only to mounted-trait (vehicle) weapons, representing that a building-scale creature shrugs off car-mounted guns the way a tank shrugs off rifle fire; (c) vehicle weapons retuned from Moderate to GM Core's own Low tier for support combatants (+20/3d6+10 instead of +24/3d8+12). Plus two new vehicle-exclusive actions: Spot (buffs an ally's next attack — the actual mechanism for 'vehicles enable Frames to become optimal Claimant-defeating tools') and Evacuate (contributes to the Shelter Evacuation pool, must be 30ft+ from the Claimant — a real trade-off between fighting and protecting civilians directly).

The arrival-wave table's first draft put the Frame at Round 6 (a literal ~20mph walking-pace conversion). Running the fully-wired simulation exposed that this was too late in practice: an 8-round fight gave the Frame exactly one round of action, by which point two vehicles' five uncontested rounds had already taken the Claimant most of the way to 0 HP — the SAME 'vehicles win, Frame irrelevant' failure this whole section exists to fix, just relocated from per-hit damage to rounds of uncontested access. REVISED 2026-08-22, same day: Frame now arrives Round 3 (still after all-but-two vehicles, still a real 'vehicles hold the line alone first' beat, but with real rounds left to be decisive). Re-simulated result: Frame 73 damage (the single largest contributor, 44% of the Claimant's 165 HP), vehicles 103 combined across three combatants with none individually outdamaging the Frame, Spot fired once, Evacuate got 10 civilians clear. This is the balance the original ask was for.

Was the field-break (data/subsystems/day-1-ground-layer.json's Field Integrity pool) a real roll or a scripted assumption in the simulator? RESOLVED 2026-08-22, design doc §14e: it's now a real roll. tools/character-builder/ extracts and re-derives six real level-1 SF2E character stat blocks (one per Player Core class) from the game's own shipped Adventure Pregens compendium — a from-scratch chargen engine (derive.mjs) verified against every pregen's own published HP total, plus the faster pregen-borrowing shortcut it powers. tools/battle-simulator/ground-layer/ rolls five of those six kids against the subsystem's real DC 15 obstacles to decide whether and when the Interdiction Field actually breaks, replacing the prior flat 'ground team did their job at round 2' assumption — including the real possibility it never breaks within the 3-round window at all.

Four more asked directly by Ingram, all resolved together 2026-08-22 (design doc §14f) because each surfaced the next while being built: (1) distances are now 10x PF2e/SF2e's default (FEET_PER_SQUARE 5->50, every Speed/range/reach scaled to match) — a reskin, not a rebalance, since square-counts-per-turn are unchanged; (2) the arrivesOnRound lookup table is GONE, replaced by real Round 0 deployment (party together at the offshore fort/downtown, Claimant a real distance away in the foothills) and real per-round movement — a strictly better fix for the same 'don't simulate 100+ rounds of literal travel' problem §14a first solved, now that distance and Speed share one rescale; (3) initiative is a real d20+modifier roll (Player Core pg. 427), not scenario array order, with vehicles using their own Reflex (GM Core pg. 236: a vehicle pilot rolls Piloting for initiative) and the reference Frame deliberately given a LOW, distinct-from-its-Reflex-save initiativeModifier (10) so it's statistically worse at initiative than the agile vehicles across 30 test seeds — 'most Frames are lumbering,' a differently-built agile-mech archetype could set this near 20; (4) every turn now closes with an action-point ledger (available/spent/held/reason) that THROWS if the numbers don't add up, and the replay UI grew a real character-sheet panel per acting combatant so every number in the narration is traceable. Building Round 0 deployment surfaced two real, previously-invisible bugs in the party AI's movement heuristic (a flat-distance budget miscalculation, and zero real sidestep options on a purely orthogonal approach) — both only mattered once combatants started far enough apart for the flaws to have room to bite.

Ingram asked directly whether the Claimant was an actual threat, and to re-verify SF2E rules as law rather than recall — RESOLVED 2026-08-22, design doc §14g, with a real confirmed rules gap found in the process: range-increment penalties (Player Core pg. 254's -2/-4/-6... per increment) were never implemented, only the hard 6th-increment cutoff — exactly how a helicopter landed an 'impossibly far' hit. Fixed, plus vehicle weapon ranges corrected to real unscaled SF2E catalog numbers (60-100ft, not 10x'd with the map) and two vehicles gained a limited-use long-range weapon (usesRemaining, a new general mechanism). The Claimant dealt 0 damage in every prior run (its 3rd action, after Advance's 2, was hardcoded to do nothing) — fixed so it Strikes anything Large+ left in reach after Advancing; verified across 8 seeds it now lands real damage every time. Fixing that surfaced a WORSE problem via a 20-seed statistical check: 13/20 seeds ground out to a helpless one-sided grind once the ground team's field-break roll failed outright (a real, designed possible outcome) — fixed with a new honest 'stalemate' outcome that ends the fight once the field is permanently unbreakable rather than grinding out rounds that can't change the result (with its own sub-bug found and fixed: it must wait for the ground team's real 3-round window to actually play out first). Open, flagged but NOT retuned without being asked: the ground team's field-break rate came out to only 30% across that same 20-seed check — a real number, not obviously a bug, but worth a decision. Also fixed while actually looking at the rendered output rather than trusting the code: Round 0 deployment tokens were visually overlapping despite occupying distinct squares (spacing widened 1->2 squares), and the active-combatant ring was sweeping an arc across the whole map instead of spinning in place (missing `transform-box:fill-box` on an SVG transform-origin).

A battle-log screenshot raised 'why did the Claimant strike when nothing looked in reach,' which Ingram escalated mid-turn into a much larger ask: 'the best possible system for automating SF2E combats... good ways to generate decisions that work towards either the enemies goals or the players.' RESOLVED 2026-08-22, design doc §14h: a shared utility-AI framework (ai/considerations.mjs's expected-value math, reusing the engine's own degreeOfSuccess directly; ai/candidates.mjs's legality-filtered candidate generation; ai/profiles.mjs's named weight tables; ai/utility-ai.mjs's score-and-pick orchestrator) now drives BOTH sides — claimant-ai.mjs and party-ai.mjs are thin wrappers over the same function, differing only by weight profile. Two capability flags (Runabout's new canEvacuate, the Ladle's existing repairBonus) replaced id-based role checks. A limited-use weapon needed a real 'reserve price' (must clear double the best free alternative's value), not just marginal-value subtraction, to honestly express Ingram's 'terrible waste if they miss' conservation intent rather than firing it for any positive edge. A first statistical re-check (this project's now-standard practice) caught two real, high-impact, pre-existing bugs the new framework's more varied movement finally exposed: computeDestination could return a bent-path destination the engine's single-straight-hop legality check would then reject outright, and every move candidate ignored feet already spent earlier the same turn — both fixed, reverified at zero illegal-action proposals across 20 seeds with the outcome split (6 victory/14 stalemate) and damage totals unchanged from §14g's baseline. The other half of the original ask — visually confirming actions land sensibly — shipped as a decision overlay on the artifact's map (move lines, hit/crit/miss-colored strike lines, a weapon-range ring), with its feet-to-pixel geometry pulled into a real, independently-tested module (artifact/geometry.mjs) rather than left as untestable inline script, specifically because a silent scale bug there would defeat the point of building it. Open, flagged but NOT changed without being asked: checkMoveLegality caps a combatant's WHOLE TURN at one Speed regardless of how many separate Move actions fund it, which real SF2E rules don't require (Stride is repeatable, each for a full Speed) — likely why so many turns in the 20-seed check held with nothing to do; whether that's a deliberate simplification or a fidelity gap is the same kind of rules-law-vs-bent-law call §14g already reserved for Ingram.

Ingram asked directly to read through a real battle transcript rather than trust the aggregate stats — 'go through the log of your last simulation, it's a hilarious mess, it needs fixing' — plus a precise spec for how the roster should be built: 'start with everyone on the field, that's 0, then roll initiative on each character, then organise the roster based on this order, then walk through the simulation.' RESOLVED 2026-08-22, design doc §14i, two real bugs found by actually reading a full transcript that §14h's statistical check had no way to catch: (1) the artifact's roster panel and Round 0 deployment listing showed scenario-authoring order while the initiative strip correctly showed the real rolled order — log.roster was built by iterating scenario.combatants instead of the initiativeOrder computed one line earlier; fixed at the source (roster construction now iterates initiativeOrder, so every display inherits the fix via normal object key ordering, no per-panel patch needed). (2) Kingfisher spent entire 5-round battles oscillating between two fixed points ~2500ft apart, moving its full Speed budget every turn and never once landing a hit — every move was individually legal, so it showed up in neither illegal-action counts nor (by itself) obviously-wrong damage totals. Root cause: computeDestination's post-§14h extend() walked a fixed compass direction for the WHOLE budget regardless of whether continuing still helped, sailing past the point of closest approach on any target not exactly on one of 8 headings, then overshooting the other way the next round when it recomputed. Fixed by refusing a step that doesn't strictly reduce distance to the target. Reverified: outcome split (6/14) and zero-illegal-actions unchanged from §14h's baseline, but now every party combatant carrying a weapon deals real average damage across a 20-seed batch (previously Kingfisher's real contribution in the traced seed was zero, invisible in the prior aggregate check because other combatants compensated). The standing lesson, now written into the battle-sim statistical-verification practice: a multi-seed statistical check proves the fight's aggregate SHAPE is right; it cannot prove any one combatant's turn-by-turn behavior makes sense, because 'always legal, always pointless' produces no signal a stat check is looking for — both a statistical check AND a full single-transcript read-through are required going forward, not either alone.

Ingram asked directly whether the simulator's combatants can cast spells, know a spell list, or use a character ability — 'we need to define roles, abilities, spells and start giving the players options' — plus a concrete validation demand: 'a system that only validates if everyone uses 100% of their actions.' RESOLVED 2026-08-22, design doc §14j (the audit) and §14k (spells/abilities). §14j: analysis/action-utilization.mjs classifies every held action point via engine.mjs's own heldReason strings into legitimate (Stunned, dead mid-turn, a real damage-state action-cap drop) vs noActionFound/illegalProposal (the gap this exists to surface) — real baseline for the escort scenario: 54.3% utilization, 19/35 turns held for no legitimate reason, every combatant affected including the Frame. §14k: every combatant previously had only weapon Strikes and a few generic vehicle actions; now a real spellAttack and healAbility action type exist end to end (legality.mjs's checkSpellAttackLegal/checkHealAbilityLegal/checkSpellRange, reusing resolveStrike directly for spell-attack resolution since Player Core's ranged-spell-attack math is identical to a Strike's). Content is REAL, not invented — Eldritch Lance and Transfer Vitality extracted via tools/pack-extractor/ from the level-1 Mystic pregen in gamesystems/sf2e/packs/paizo-pregens (the same mechanism the kid fixtures already use), scaled to level 12 via GM Core pg. 126's real Spell DC/Attack table (High tier, DC 32/+24) and the spells' own printed Heightened text. candidates.mjs unifies strikes and spells into one attack pool (collectAttackOptions) so §14h's reserve-price conservation logic covers limited-use spells automatically, no parallel mechanism needed; a new HYBRID_CASTER profile fixes ATTACKER's repair:0 silently making a heal ability un-choosable. Two real bugs found and fixed: a test-helper bug (a missing ...overrides spread silently collided two combatants onto the same id) and a genuine engine bug (mid-turn action-cap re-derivation, built in §14g/§14i to catch a reaction SHRINKING the cap, had no floor against a self-heal GROWING it back mid-turn, letting a combatant spend a 4th action point the turn never started with — accountForActions correctly caught it as a real overspend; fixed by clamping the mid-turn value at the turn's own starting budget, matching the real SF2E rule that a turn's action budget is fixed the moment it begins). A real interpretive finding, resolved but flagged: Eldritch Lance's authentic 30ft range is shorter than one grid square at this map's established 10x rescale — rescaled 10x anyway (30ft->300ft, Transfer Vitality 60ft->600ft) on the design bible's own explicit textual support ('a spell is a kilometre-wide effect'), diverging deliberately from the vehicle-weapon precedent (§14g) that keeps mundane gun ranges real — Ingram's to revisit if he disagrees. A dedicated scenarios/mystic-frame-solo.mjs scenario (a solo 1v1, no support) verified across 20 seeds: 122 spell casts, 38 heals, zero illegal proposals, 69.0% utilization (up from 54.3%) on a fixture with exactly two real abilities — the remaining gap is honestly explained (a full level-12 PC has far more than two known actions; this fixture proves the system, not a complete character sheet) rather than hidden. Verified both statistically AND by reading a full real transcript end to end, per §14i's own standing lesson. 280/280 tests passing project-wide.

Ingram asked directly for the six kids and six Frames to get real names, classes, and Anchors ('the most fully we simulate things the better'), plus a UI section explaining WHY an action was chosen alongside WHAT happened, visualized as boxes sized to each action's real point cost. RESOLVED 2026-08-22, design doc §14l (characters) and §14m (UI). §14l: every other layer of this project's own documentation (CLAUDE.md, data/characters/*/README.md, build-kid-fixture.mjs's own header comment) flags naming the six as collaborative work reserved for Ingram — proceeded given his direct instruction, but every file is marked DRAFT/open to full revision, not a lock-in. The six kids are built via tools/character-builder/derive.mjs directly (Human ancestry, not the pregen shortcut, since all six real Adventure Pregens turned out to be non-human sci-fi ancestries — a mismatch for 1950s Japan) with real Anchors grounded in campaign-arc.md's own tone section, including one kid (Kaneda Masaru / Yoon Jae-won) carrying a zainichi Korean identity thread reflecting the setting's own explicit ask for complexity beyond generic-Japan. The six Frames are grounded in GM Core's real level-12 creature-building tables (AC/attack/damage/saves/perception/HP, pg. 121-126, cited directly), each with one signature ability (the same scope precedent as the Mystic Frame test fixture) rather than a full feat-complete build; Tsukikage reuses the exact same pack-extracted Eldritch Lance/Transfer Vitality content already proven in the battle simulator. Every kid pilots a Frame of a DIFFERENT class (full 6-class permutation) as a deliberate point of narrative contrast. All twelve files validate against schema AND pass through the real Foundry Actor-data generators via the existing generic data-corpus test, with zero new tests needed. §14m: decisionReason (real data since §14h/§14k) was never actually shown anywhere in the UI — fixed with a new Roleplaying & Decision-Making panel: a round overview (every combatant's turn so far, one row each, boxes sized by real action-point cost via a newly-added engine.mjs actionsCost field on every logged action) plus a Why This Turn block giving full reasoning text. Two real bugs found and fixed in the process: actionCost() was a hardcoded per-type table that didn't know spellAttack/healAbility have variable costs (undersizing a 2-action spell's box to look like a 1-action Move — fixed at the engine source, not patched in the UI), and the scenario tab bar was hardcoded to two buttons, silently leaving the mystic-frame-solo scenario (added in §14k) unreachable from the UI at all — fixed by generating tabs from RUNS.runs' own keys. Verified in-browser: a real 7-combatant round renders as 7 rows, with Kingfisher's three separate moves (§14i) showing as three genuinely separate boxes in order, confirming Ingram's 'three separate move actions, three separate arrows' ask structurally rather than by assumption. Scoped out, flagged rather than rushed: full token-position animation ('tokens actually move around... at a measured pace... replay the turn') is a genuinely separate front-end task (position interpolation, pacing controls, reconciling with the existing instant-jump scrubber) — not attempted this pass. 282/282 tests passing project-wide.
